It makes sense to feel nervous. Choosing a career can sound as if you’re picking one path for the rest of your life, but most people make smaller decisions, learn from them, and adjust. You don’t need to discover a perfect calling before you can take a useful next step.

Try treating career choices as experiments rather than permanent commitments. Notice what matters to you in everyday work: solving problems, helping people, making things, having variety, working independently, earning stability, or having time outside work. Then look for a role that offers some of those things, rather than expecting one job to meet every need. Talking with people in different fields, doing a short project, volunteering, or taking an introductory course can give you real information without requiring a major commitment.

It may also help to separate what you enjoy from what you’re good at and what you need. Those can overlap, but they don’t have to match perfectly. A job can be worthwhile because it provides income and stability while you explore interests elsewhere; work doesn’t have to be your whole identity.

If you choose something and later find it doesn’t suit you, that isn’t proof you’ve failed or wasted your time. You’ll have learned which tasks, environments, or conditions fit you better, and many skills transfer across fields. You can make the decision more manageable by choosing a next step for the coming few months, then checking in with yourself about what you learned.

You’re not behind if you don’t have a clear answer yet. Aim for a reasonable next move, not certainty about your entire future.

Most colleges have several kinds of support, though the names and availability vary. Start with your instructor or teaching assistant: office hours are specifically for questions, and you can ask for help before you feel completely behind. Many schools also offer tutoring centers, study groups, writing or math support, and peer-led review sessions.

For guidance beyond coursework, look for academic advising, first-year programs, mentoring, and student-success or counseling services. Some departments pair students with faculty or peer mentors; others expect you to request one. You can ask admissions or the advising office what is available and how to sign up before the term begins. A resident adviser, if you live on campus, can also help you find the right office.

At a large college, support may not arrive automatically, so reaching out early matters. You do not need to have a serious problem to ask a question. Try sending a short message such as, “I’m having trouble with this topic—could you suggest a good next step?” Many students feel uncertain at first, and using campus resources is a normal part of college.

You don’t need to settle on one permanent career goal before you can make progress. Start by separating goals into time horizons: what you want to learn or try soon, what kind of work and life you might want in a few years, and the broader values you want your life to reflect. Those values might include creativity, stability, helping others, independence, or time for family. They can guide you even while the job title is unclear.

Then look for clues in your everyday experience. Which tasks hold your attention? What do people ask you for help with? Which parts of school, work, or volunteering leave you satisfied, and which consistently drain you? You could also talk with people in different roles, take a short course, volunteer, or try a small project. Treat each as an experiment, not a commitment.

Set a near-term goal based on what you can test—for example, exploring two fields this month or building one relevant skill. Review what you learn and adjust. Uncertainty doesn’t mean you lack ambition; it often means you need more information. Goals can evolve as you gain experience.

It sounds as though you have already made an important shift: you are starting to separate what other people value from what genuinely interests you. That does not mean you need to identify one perfect career immediately. Careers are rarely a single right answer waiting to be discovered; they are paths you can test, adjust, and build over time.

Try turning “technological innovation and entrepreneurship” into questions you can investigate. Which problems or fields interest you? Do you enjoy building products, writing code, designing experiences, researching, selling, or organizing a team? Entrepreneurship involves more than having ideas: it can mean uncertainty, customer conversations, budgeting, persistence, and taking responsibility when plans change. Some of those realities may appeal to you more than others, and that is useful information.

Look for low-risk ways to try the work before making a major commitment. Take a practical course, build a small project, join a student team, volunteer with a startup, or interview people in roles that interest you. Pay attention not just to whether the work sounds exciting, but to how you feel while doing its ordinary parts. A career should fit your interests, but also your strengths, preferred work environment, financial needs, and tolerance for risk.

It may also help to distinguish the kind of impact you want from the job title you imagine. “Innovation” could lead to engineering, product management, design, research, business development, or founding a company. You do not have to start a business right away to pursue entrepreneurship; learning how organizations identify needs, make products, and serve customers can be a strong foundation.

Finally, give yourself permission to change direction as you learn. Choosing a first course of study or role is not a lifelong contract. Talk with people whose work you are curious about, ask what their typical week is really like, and compare several options rather than relying on anyone else’s definition of success. The goal is not to prove that your choice is right once and for all, but to make the next informed move toward work that feels meaningful and sustainable to you.

Passion is not always something you discover in a sudden, unmistakable moment. Often it develops as you learn more, build skills, and find out what kinds of problems you enjoy working on. You don’t need to know your lifelong calling before choosing a next step.

I can help you think through career options, though I can’t replace a career counselor who knows your circumstances. Since you’re interested in science and technology, start by looking for the specific activities that appeal to you. Do you like asking why things happen, doing experiments, solving mathematical problems, building or fixing things, writing code, designing products, helping people use technology, or explaining ideas? “Science and technology” covers many different kinds of work, and the day-to-day tasks matter more than the field’s label.

Try a few small, low-cost experiments before making a big commitment. Take an introductory course, do a beginner project, visit a science or technology event, or speak with someone studying or working in an area you’re curious about. After each experience, note what interested you, what frustrated you, and whether you wanted to keep going even when it became difficult. Enjoyment doesn’t mean every task is fun; it often means the challenging parts still feel worthwhile.

It may also help to consider practical preferences: how much schooling you’re willing to pursue, whether you prefer working with people or independently, whether you enjoy hands-on or abstract work, and what kinds of jobs are available where you live. For example, someone drawn to biology and data might explore bioinformatics; someone who likes building and physics might investigate engineering; someone who enjoys logic and creating digital tools might try software development. These are possibilities to test, not conclusions about what you should do.

If you share your age or education level, the science or technology subjects you enjoy most, and a few activities you dislike or find difficult, I can suggest a more tailored set of career paths and ways to explore them.

You do not need a long work history to apply for an entry-level job. “Experience” can include responsibilities from school, volunteering, clubs, sports, family activities, or helping with events—not just paid employment. Look for roles that commonly hire teenagers, such as grocery or retail work, food service, recreation programs, tutoring, or seasonal positions. Some listings describe an ideal candidate rather than a strict requirement, so consider applying if you meet the essential qualifications. Check your local rules for working minors, including permitted hours and tasks, and ask a parent or guardian to help you understand them.

Keep your first résumé simple and to one page. Put your name, phone number, and a professional email at the top; you do not need to include your age, birth date, photo, or full home address. Add a short objective if it helps—for example, that you are a reliable student seeking an entry-level position and are available at particular times. Then include your education, relevant activities or volunteer work, skills, and any responsibilities that show reliability. Describe what you actually did: “helped organize a school fundraiser and handled setup” is more useful than simply listing “fundraiser.” Don’t claim skills or experience you don’t have, and ask permission before listing someone as a reference.

You can prepare by practicing a brief introduction, filling out a sample application, and thinking of examples that show you are dependable, cooperative, and willing to learn. Ask a teacher, coach, or volunteer supervisor whether they would be comfortable serving as a reference. Have someone proofread your résumé, and make sure your voicemail greeting and email address are appropriate.

Apply through employers’ official websites or in person when appropriate, and follow each employer’s instructions. If you do not hear back, a polite follow-up after a reasonable interval is fine. A first job is partly about learning: punctuality, asking questions when instructions are unclear, communicating schedule conflicts early, and accepting feedback matter as much as prior experience.

It’s okay not to have your whole career figured out before choosing a major. Start by narrowing things down: Which subjects do you enjoy, which are you good at, and what kinds of work would you like to try? Also consider practical factors such as program requirements, cost, and how easily you could change majors later.

If the deadline is close, look at the majors that keep several paths open, and check whether your college offers a general or exploratory program. Talk to an academic adviser as soon as possible; they can explain which courses count toward multiple majors and what happens if you decide to switch. You might also ask a trusted teacher or someone working in a field you’re curious about what the day-to-day work is really like.

Try not to choose only because someone else expects it, or because you feel one decision determines your whole life. Many people change direction. For now, make the best informed choice you can, and focus on taking introductory courses that help you learn what fits.

Architecture calls for a mix of creative, technical, and people skills. You’ll need to develop visual thinking, drawing and design judgment, and the ability to turn ideas into practical plans that meet safety rules, budgets, and clients’ needs. Clear communication, collaboration, time management, and openness to feedback matter too. Software skills can be learned; curiosity, persistence, and attention to detail are just as valuable.

You may not need to choose one passion and leave the others behind. First, look for the kind of workday you want: creating things, helping people, solving problems, collaborating, or having predictable hours. Then explore roles that combine your interests, such as art therapy, music education, user research, community arts, or marketing for creative organizations. These are starting points to investigate, not commitments.

Try small, low-risk experiments before making a big decision: take a short course, volunteer, shadow someone, or do a small project. Pay attention not only to whether the subject is interesting, but also whether you enjoy the everyday tasks and working conditions. Talking with people in a few different roles can reveal what their jobs are actually like.

You can also choose a practical first step rather than a lifelong identity. Skills and interests can develop, and many careers leave room for creative work or helping others outside the job. Aim for a direction you’re curious enough to test, then reassess as you learn more.

A useful career choice is less about finding one perfect calling and more about finding work that fits your priorities and circumstances reasonably well. Consider what you enjoy doing, but also what you are good at, what you are willing to learn, and which everyday tasks you can tolerate. The reality of a job can differ from its image: someone may love a subject but dislike the routine work involved in that field.

Think about your preferred lifestyle, too. Pay, stability, hours, location, flexibility, physical demands, and time for family or other interests all matter. Decide which are essential and which are negotiable. Research typical working conditions and career progression, not just starting salaries or success stories.

You do not have to make a lifelong decision immediately. Talk with people doing the work, try a short course, volunteer, shadow someone, or take an entry-level role if you can. These small experiments can reveal whether you like the day-to-day reality before you commit to extensive training. Also consider the cost and time required to qualify, and whether the skills you gain can transfer to other roles.

Finally, separate your own preferences from expectations imposed by family, peers, or social status. A good path is one you can sustain and adapt as you learn more. Choosing a direction is a starting point, not a promise that you can never change it.

Your AOS would qualify you to start building practical experience, and that experience can help you decide whether management is a goal you actually want. Consider working for a few years, then pursuing the BBA part-time or with employer support if it fits your plans. A degree may help with supervision or operations roles, but it doesn’t guarantee better pay or options; hands-on skill, certifications, and reliability matter too.

Before deciding, compare the programs’ total cost, transfer credits, and likely entry-level wages, and ask local employers what they value for advancement. Also treat “guaranteed jobs” as a possibility rather than a promise: demand varies by location, specialty, and economic conditions.

The major’s label usually matters less than the skills and experience you build. A general biology degree can keep options open, while a specialty can help you focus—but neither guarantees a job. Look at course requirements and local job postings, and consider internships, research, lab techniques, statistics, or programming. If you’re unsure, start broad and specialize through electives or research; check whether switching later would delay graduation.

You don’t need to settle on a career direction to find a summer job. Start with roles that hire people without experience and fit your schedule: retail, food service, recreation programs, camps, tutoring, lifeguarding (if certified), or seasonal work. Look for phrases like “training provided,” “entry-level,” and “no experience required,” and check local employers’ age requirements.

Apply to jobs that interest you, but tailor each application to show reliability, communication, teamwork, or relevant school and volunteer activities. Ask a school counselor, family member, or local community organization about openings, too. Internships are often aimed at college students, but regular summer jobs are a good way to build experience.

It’s understandable to feel disoriented after graduating, especially when the job search is taking longer than expected. Start with your college’s career services office, which may offer appointments to alumni, résumé reviews, and practice interviews. You could also ask a former professor, internship supervisor, or someone working in a field you’re considering for a short conversation about their path and the skills employers seek. If you’re unsure what direction to take, a career counselor can help you explore options and set practical next steps. For now, choose one small weekly goal, such as contacting two people or applying to a few well-matched roles.

Include your contact information, a brief summary tailored to the role, relevant work or volunteer experience, education, and skills that match the job description. For each role, describe what you did and what changed as a result; use specific examples or numbers where you can. Include projects, certifications, or activities that show useful abilities, especially if you have limited work experience. Keep the layout clear, proofread carefully, and leave out unrelated details. No resume can guarantee a job, so tailor each application honestly to the position.

Keep it to one page and tailor it to each role. Put education, technical skills, and projects or experience where they’re easy to find. For each project, briefly state what you built, the tools used, and the result or your contribution. Use clear action verbs, quantify impact when possible, and proofread carefully. Don’t list skills you can’t discuss in an interview.

A decade without engineering employment is a serious hurdle, but it does not mean your prospects are permanently poisoned. It does mean that sending more applications with the same approach is unlikely to change the result. The immediate goal is to find out where your applications are falling out and build recent, credible evidence that you can do the work.

Ask a few engineers or recruiters in your specific discipline to review your résumé against actual entry-level postings. ATS compatibility is only one issue: employers may see an old degree and no recent engineering projects or experience, and pass before an interview. Make your target narrow—one discipline, relevant roles, and realistic locations—and tailor the résumé to each posting. Your other jobs are not disqualifying; describe transferable skills such as troubleshooting, documentation, safety, and reliability, without letting them dominate the page.

Look for a bridge into the field: technician, engineering assistant, CAD, quality, test, manufacturing, or contract roles, as well as internships that accept graduates. A small portfolio of relevant projects, a volunteer project with a concrete deliverable, or current software/tool training can help show recent capability. These are most useful when aligned with jobs you are actually targeting, rather than as more unrelated certificates.

Try informational conversations with alumni, local engineering societies, and hiring managers; referrals can help your application get reviewed. If possible, ask for a candid résumé review and feedback on a few specific applications before sending another large batch.

A minor can give your degree useful breadth or depth, especially when it complements your major. It may help you explore an interest, build skills relevant to a career, or show employers how your studies connect across fields. But it is rarely as important as your major, experience, and demonstrated abilities. Choose one if the coursework genuinely supports your goals or interests, not simply to collect another credential.

Starting early is useful, but you don’t need to build a professional network before you’ve begun college. Focus first on learning what kinds of work interest you: research, conservation, fisheries, environmental consulting, aquariums, government, or marine technology all use marine biology in different ways.

Your combination of marine biology and data science could be especially valuable. Build skills in statistics, coding, geographic information systems (GIS), data visualization, and clear scientific writing, then use class projects or personal projects to show how you apply them to real questions. A small, well-documented project can be a good conversation starter.

Once in college, ask professors and teaching assistants about research opportunities, and look for internships, field courses, lab assistant roles, and volunteer work with local conservation groups, museums, aquariums, or environmental agencies. Attend public talks and student or professional events, and follow organizations’ newsletters and job postings to learn what skills they seek. When contacting someone, be specific: briefly explain your interests, mention something relevant about their work, and ask one focused question rather than requesting a job or a broad mentorship.

Keep records of projects, fieldwork, and skills. Experience and relationships tend to grow through consistent, useful contributions—not networking for its own sake.

Studying abroad can be a great choice if it fits your goals and finances. It can help you become more independent, experience another culture, and build language or professional skills. Before deciding, compare the total cost, check whether credits will transfer, and consider how the program aligns with your degree or career plans. You don’t need to go abroad to have a strong education, but a well-chosen program can be valuable. Short exchanges or summer programs may offer a lower-cost way to try it.
